When traders look for a powerful charting and analysis tool, the **[TradingView](https://in.tradingview.com/?aff_id=167054) vs Thinkorswim** debate often comes up. Both platforms have loyal followings, but they serve slightly different needs. This guide breaks down the strengths, weaknesses, pricing, and ideal use cases so you can decide which one fits your trading style.

## Platform Overview
### TradingView Basics
TradingView is a web‑based charting suite known for its intuitive interface and vibrant social community. Traders can access it from any browser, create custom indicators with Pine Script, and share ideas instantly. The platform supports stocks, forex, crypto, futures, and more, making it a versatile choice for retail traders who value visual analysis and collaboration.

### Thinkorswim Basics
Thinkorswim (often abbreviated TOS) is the desktop‑focused platform offered by TD Ameritrade (now part of Charles Schwab). It combines advanced charting, professional‑grade tools, and paper trading in a single downloadable application. Thinkorswim is favored by active traders who need deep analytics, complex order types, and direct market access through a brokerage account.

## Feature Comparison
### Charting Tools
TradingView shines with over 100 built‑in studies, dozens of chart types, and seamless multi‑timeframe layouts. Its drawing tools are drag‑and‑drop simple, and the community publishes thousands of public scripts. Thinkorswim offers equally robust charting, including thinkScript for custom studies, but the interface feels more traditional and can be overwhelming for newcomers. Both platforms support multiple chart linking, but TradingView’s cloud sync gives you instant access from any device.

### Order Types & Execution
Thinkorswim excels when it comes to order sophistication. You can place conditional orders, OCO (one‑cancels‑other), brackets, and even algo‑style strategies directly from the chart. Execution is routed through TD Ameritrade’s infrastructure, providing reliable fills for equities, options, and futures. TradingView, while excellent for analysis, relies on broker integrations for order placement. You can connect to many brokers, but the native order entry is less granular than Thinkorswim’s built‑in ticket system.

### Community & Social
One of TradingView’s biggest draws is its social feed. Traders publish ideas, comment on charts, and follow each other like a mini‑social network. This environment fosters learning and idea generation, especially for beginners. Thinkorswim has a community forum and chat rooms, but the interaction is more formal and less integrated into the charting experience. If you value crowd‑sourced insights, TradingView has the edge.

## Pricing
### TradingView Pricing
TradingView offers a free tier with limited indicators and one chart per layout. Paid plans start at $14.95/month (Pro), $29.95/month (Pro+), and $49.95/month (Premium). Higher tiers unlock more charts per layout, additional server‑side alerts, and priority customer support. All plans are billed monthly or annually with a discount for yearly commitment.

### Thinkorswim Pricing
Thinkorswim itself is free to use if you have a funded TD Ameritrade/Charles Schwab account. There are no platform fees, but you pay standard commissions and fees for trades (which have been $0 for online stock and ETF trades since 2019). Options and futures still incur per‑contract fees. Because the platform is tied to a brokerage, there’s no separate subscription cost, making it attractive for cost‑conscious active traders.

## Pros & Cons
### TradingView Pros/Cons
**Pros:**  
- Intuitive, modern UI  
- Powerful Pine Script for custom studies  
- Strong social community and idea sharing  
- Cloud‑based access from any device  
- Flexible broker integrations  

**Cons:**  
- Order execution depends on third‑party brokers  
- Free version limited to one chart per
